item.title: [AJLS] #ENDSARS: Public Protest against Human Rights Abuses, Police Brutality and Predatory Policing in Nigeria
item.dc:creator: Fidelia U. Nwome, Chijioke Egwu Ekumaoko, Ozioma Victoria Uchime
item.description: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title> <jats:p> Police brutality is a pervasive problem that impedes human rights in many societies. In Nigeria, the level of police brutality is alarmingly high, leaving citizens in fear of contact with the police. Beyond colonial legacies, factors such as poor funding and training, lack of accountability mechanisms, and inadequate punitive measures sustain the persistence of police brutality. This study interrogates the use of excessive force by Nigeria’s Special Anti-Robbery Squad ( <jats:sc>SARS</jats:sc> ), which restricts public civic space and violates human rights. Using a qualitative methodology, and drawing from primary data collected from Amnesty International reports and interviews with key informants such as security agents, legal practitioners, and ordinary citizens, including victims of <jats:sc>SARS</jats:sc> brutality, the study highlights human rights abuses by the <jats:sc>SARS</jats:sc> . The findings indicate that <jats:sc>SARS</jats:sc> has conspicuously deviated from its original duty of combating crime to perpetrating and abetting crime and violence against the public, particularly Nigerian youth. This situation urgently demands redress. </jats:p>

item.title: [AJLS] Nigerian Asylum Seekers in the United States: the Challenge of Credibility Assessments in the Age of Digital Evidence
item.dc:creator: Philippa Osim Inyang
item.description: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title> <jats:p> Nigerian citizens fleeing insurgent violence or anti- <jats:sc>LGBTQ</jats:sc> + laws form a growing cohort of U.S. asylum applicants, yet their claims often turn on credibility assessments shaped by evidentiary gaps. Digital evidence, social media activity, messaging records, and online traces, offer new avenues for corroboration but also introduce risks of misinterpretation, privacy intrusion, and structural bias, particularly for individuals who conceal their identities to survive. This article investigates the U.S. legal framework governing credibility determinations under the <jats:sc>REAL ID</jats:sc> Act and key decisions such as <jats:italic>Matter of A-B-</jats:italic> , analysing how digital expectations intersect with the lived realities of applicants fleeing Boko Haram and persecution under Nigeria’s Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act of 2013. Drawing on international human rights standards, including the <jats:sc>UNCHR</jats:sc> Handbook and the <jats:sc>ICCPR</jats:sc> , it argues that digital evidence has become a decisive, and sometimes distorting, force in asylum adjudication and offers reforms to ensure more context-sensitive and rights-consistent credibility assessments. </jats:p>

item.title: [AJLS] Potential of Using Cultural Artefacts to Enhance the Critical Study of International Law in Africa
item.dc:creator: Babatunde Fagbayibo
item.description: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title> <jats:p>This article examines the role cultural artefacts can play in counteracting the systemic erasure of non-European ideational iterations in international law. Cultural artefacts, in both physical and digital/pictorial forms, are valuable tools for enhancing learners’ cognitive abilities. In the context of international law, cultural artefacts can elicit the critique of hegemonic discourses, emphasising the imperative of engaging other disciplines in addressing critical issues, and encouraging the development of new terminologies for expanding the ideational parameters of the discipline. In order to achieve these lofty goals, international law teachers must be intentional about identifying the relevant artefacts and incorporating them into learning activities that equip learners with critical intellectual capacities. Such engagement not only centres learners’ cultural worldview in the learning environment but also makes them active thought leaders and change agents.</jats:p>

item.title: [AJLS] Arguing for Judicial Expropriation in Cases of Unenforceable Eviction Orders
item.dc:creator: Tanveer Rashid Jeewa
item.description: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title> <jats:p> Unlawful occupation has recently peaked due to the slow pace of South Africa’s provision of housing and the private sector’s inability to cater to poor and vulnerable people. When unlawful occupation is not curbed on private land, two rights are in conflict: the right of unlawful occupiers not to be arbitrarily evicted from their homes and the right of property owners not to be arbitrarily deprived of their property, except through the operation of a law of general application. Unlawful occupation creates a lacuna, as existing remedies often fail to resolve the conflict without unduly limiting the rights of the parties. Relying on the cases of <jats:italic>President and Another v Modderklip Boerdery (Pty) Ltd</jats:italic> and <jats:italic>Fischer v Persons Listed</jats:italic> , I argue that exceptional circumstances call for judicial expropriation, which is a just and equitable order under section 172(1)(b) of the Constitution that does not breach the doctrine of separation of powers. </jats:p>

item.title: [AJLS] Interface of Customary Institutions and State Laws in Rangeland Administration in Oromia, Ethiopia
item.dc:creator: Fekadu Beyene Kenee, Gadissa Tesfaye, Jebessa Teshome
item.description: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title> <jats:p>This paper examines state-customary law relations with respect to rangeland administration among pastoralists and agro-pastoralists in the Oromia region of Ethiopia. It relies on socioeconomic data from four locations, using mixed methods to capture diverse perspectives. The findings indicate that customary-state relations have become complex due to land use change and state interventions. The strength and functioning of customary institutions vary across pastoral groups. While their role is declining over time, some still strongly influence rangeland administration. The factors that determine their influence include observance of indigenous norms, limited protection of pastoral systems that favour farming, resettlement of ethnic groups on territories claimed by others, certification of privately used lands, neglect of communal tenure, favouring women’s access to land, and promoting youth engagement in decision-making. The article stresses the importance of recognising customary authorities involved in the administration of rangeland resources, developing community bylaws, and empowering customary authorities to enable them to enforce communal land rights. It urges the adoption of mechanisms for state laws to accommodate customary laws, recognise youth empowerment, and promote women’s access to land and decision-making agency.</jats:p>

item.title: [PELJ] An Overview and Critique of the Labour Courts' Interpretation and Application of Protection Against <i>Indirect</i> Forms of Unfair Discrimination as Provided for in South Africa's Employment <i>Equity Act</i>
item.dc:creator: Elsabé Huysamen
item.description: Unfair discrimination is deeply woven into the fabric of South African society. In the post-apartheid constitutional era, the Constitution guarantees the right to equality in the pursuit of "the full and equal enjoyment of all rights and freedoms". This reflects the adoption of substantive equality, which goes beyond mere formal equality. The constitutional right to equality is grounded in two constitutionally mandated mechanisms: affirmative action, and the prohibition of unfair discrimination. Within the broader transformative vision of the Constitution, the prohibition of unfair discrimination plays a dual role: it serves as a baseline for the defence of formal equality; and it acts as a tool of transformation, particularly through the protection against indirect unfair discrimination. Protection against indirect unfair discrimination is also provided in section 6(1) of the Employment Equity Act. In a transformative context, protection against indirect discrimination is particularly significant because it recognises that equal treatment can sometimes perpetuate inequality. By uncovering and dismantling hidden barriers and power structures in the workplace, protection against indirect unfair discrimination plays a crucial role in fostering substantive equality and driving long-term, systemic change. Yet, despite its transformative potential, the application of protection against indirect unfair discrimination in South African labour jurisprudence has been limited. Against the aforesaid background, the article provides an overview of the approach adopted by South African labour courts to the protection against indirect unfair discrimination under South African labour law, while ultimately critiquing it.

item.title: [Obiter] Clarifying Section 2B of the Wills Act
item.dc:creator: Francois Du Toit, Cameron Finberg Steele
item.description: Case law and academic commentary on section 2B of the Wills Act are characterised by terminological and descriptive inconsistencies regarding what the provision does and how it achieves its outcome of excluding a testator's surviving former spouse from testamentary benefit. This contribution interrogates these inconsistencies and proffers answers to the questions of what section 2B does and how the provision does it. In so doing, the contribution seeks to situate section 2B correctly among the devices used in South Africa's testate succession law.

item.title: [Obiter] Guardians or Gatekeepers? A Reflection on the Role of State and Non-State Actors in Advancing the Right of Immigrant Children to Basic Education in South Africa
item.dc:creator: Bridget Joyce Machaka
item.description: The right to basic education is guaranteed in South Africa under section 29(1)(a) of the Constitution and applies to “everyone” without discrimination based on any prohibited ground. This right is universally recognised as foundational to a dignified life. However, immigrant children face significant challenges in accessing this right owing to exclusionary administrative practices, procedural barriers and inadequate policy implementation. This article explores how state and non-state actors affect the realisation of immigrant children’s right to education, either as facilitators or obstacles. State actors, such as the Department of Basic Education and school governing bodies, hold key roles in policy development, resource allocation and programming. Yet, these institutions often act as “gatekeepers”, implementing exclusionary measures that hinder access to basic education. Conversely, non-state actors often act as “guardians” by driving policy reform, holding the state accountable through advocacy and litigation. Furthermore, the judiciary plays a pivotal role as a protective mechanism, enforcing the right to basic education in multiple contexts, explaining the scope of the State’s obligations and declaring unconstitutional exclusionary policies that limit immigrant children’s learning opportunities. This is demonstrated by groundbreaking court cases such as the Centre for Child Law v Minister of Basic Education. This article argues that while these actors have significant potential to advance immigrant children’s educational rights, their actions may also perpetuate barriers. The article argues that achieving equitable access to education requires ongoing vigilance, strong collaboration among actors and across sectors, and robust monitoring and accountability mechanisms to prevent and grant effective remedies for violations of the right to education.

item.title: [Obiter] The Basic Education Laws Amendment Act of 2024: Fortifying the Legal Framework Prohibiting Corporal Punishment
item.dc:creator: Laetitia-Ann Greeff
item.description: Over the last three decades, South Africa has steadily eliminated the lawful use of corporal punishment in various settings: corporal punishment has been removed as a punishment for a crime, and as a disciplinary measure in penal institutions, independent schools (formerly private schools), state schools, alternative-care settings, and by parents and those in loco parentis. However, while corporal punishment is prohibited in all these settings, some technical issues remained to be rectified. One of those issues was the lacuna in section 10 of the Schools Act, which prohibited corporal punishment under the threat of criminal sanction without providing a clear definition of what corporal punishment entails. The South African Constitution requires a statute to be clear and unambiguous. In order to adhere to the principle of legality as set in section 35(3) of the Constitution, this defect needed to be addressed by including a comprehensive definition of the concept of corporal punishment in the Schools Act. In one of the most significant reforms to the basic education legal framework since 1994, the Basic Education Laws Amendment Act 32 of 2024 rectified this issue. It amended the Schools Act by including a clear and very wide definition of corporal punishment that is similar to the definition adopted by the Committee on the Rights of the Child in General Comment No. 8. The last issue for the South African legislature to address is the need for a statutory prohibition on corporal punishment in the home – to follow up on the Constitutional Court’s decision in Freedom of Religion South Africa v Minister of Justice and Constitutional Development – which would further strengthen the legal framework that prohibits corporal punishment across all settings. Adding a positive statement to the Children’s Act will achieve this goal.

item.title: [Obiter] The Role of Communication in Labour Dispute Resolution: Insights From the South African Context
item.dc:creator: Mahlatse Innocent Maake-Malatji, DC Machedi, M Ntatamala
item.description: Effective communication skills are crucial for trade unions if they are to represent employee interests and foster social purpose in employment relations. This study addresses the challenges posed by South Africa’s diverse workforce, cultural barriers, and restrictive legal frameworks, all of which impact the ability of unions to communicate effectively. This article is rooted in the persistent communication failures within labour disputes that have resulted in adverse outcomes, including industrial action and tragic events like the Marikana massacre. The article explores key case studies, including the 2012 Marikana miners’ strike and the 2010 municipal workers’ strike, to demonstrate how communication can escalate conflict or promote peaceful resolutions. A thorough analysis reveals that poor communication impedes negotiations and disrupts social cohesion, threatening economic stability. By contrast, effective communication, as demonstrated in the municipal workers’ strike led by the South African Municipal Workers Union, highlights the potential of trade unions to achieve favourable outcomes through media engagement, negotiation skills, and strategic public communication. The research adopts a qualitative methodology, relying on case-study analysis and regulatory frameworks governing labour relations in South Africa. Key findings indicate that trade unions face critical gaps in communication, negotiation, and conflict-resolution skills, as highlighted by the ETDP SETA report. Addressing these challenges is imperative for sustainable labour relations. This article contributes to employment relations by offering insights into how trade unions can develop communication strategies to align with a social purpose that transcends adversarial engagements. The value of the study lies in equipping unions with practical recommendations to foster cooperation, mitigate conflict, and advocate effectively for workers in diverse, multicultural work environments.

item.title: [Obiter] Unveiling Reverse Piercing: Section 20(9)(<i>a</i>) of the Companies Act 71 of 2008
item.dc:creator: Charlene Lanser
item.description: Section 20(9)(a) of the Companies Act 71 of 2008 (hereinafter referred to as the 2008 Act) in South Africa allows courts to pierce the corporate veil, disregarding the separate legal personality of a company when it constitutes unconscionable abuse by shareholders to commit fraud, avoid obligations, or engage in improper conduct. This article explores the potential interpretation of Section 20(9)(a) in reverse, allowing courts to impose an individual's liabilities onto the company, provided specific conditions are met. The concept of reverse piercing aims to prevent the misuse of company structures to evade personal liabilities or commit fraud, but it can erode the principle of limited liability and may open floodgates for unjust claims, undermining corporate stability and trust in business transactions. The doctrine of piercing the corporate veil safeguards against the misuse of a company and its form, preventing individuals from abusing limited liability protection for personal gain. It aims to strike a balance between encouraging entrepreneurship and protecting the legal system. Reverse piercing of the corporate veil is a novel legal development where liabilities of a company can be attributed directly to its individual shareholders or members. This approach is often used in scenarios where a company engages in fraudulent, wrongful, or unjust conduct. Texas law has shaped reverse piercing jurisprudence, emphasising the importance of ownership and a clear demonstration of alter ego status for reverse piercing. In re Packer and In re Juliet Homes, courts found grounds to claim non-debtor company assets through reverse piercing, provided the companies operated as alter egos of the owner-debtors. Reverse piercing of the corporate veil in Texas allows creditors to reach a company's assets to satisfy shareholders' debts, contingent on establishing an alter-ego relationship between the individual and the company. Reverse piercing, a possible legal mechanism under Sections 20(9) and 20(9)(a) of the 2008 Act, aims to hold a company liable for the actions or debts of its shareholders and/or members, rather than traditional piercing where shareholders are held liable for the company's actions. However, navigating the legal criteria for reverse piercing can be challenging, as courts must balance the need for accountability with fair treatment of corporate entities. The process can also be cumbersome and costly, and potential abuse by litigants is a concern. Corporate entities may need to revisit governance structures and practices to mitigate potential exposure to reverse piercing claims.

item.title: [Obiter] Statutory Interpretation “Laced” With a De Minimis Amount of Vanilla - Commissioner for the South African Revenue Service v Diageo SA (Pty) Ltd [2024] ZASCA 158
item.dc:creator: Silke De Lange, Monique Malan
item.description: This case note analyses and comments on the Supreme Court of Appeal’s (SCA) judgment of 15 November 2024 in Commissioner for the South African Revenue Service v Diageo SA (Pty) Ltd [2024] JOL 67602 (SCA) (SCA judgment). The dispute concerns the tariff classification of a locally manufactured liqueur, Cape Velvet Cream Original (CVCO), for purposes of determining the applicable excise duty rate. To promote the labour-intensive wine industry, a lower rate of excise duty was introduced for liqueurs containing only “wine spirits to which other non-alcoholic ingredients have been added.” CVCO is made from wine spirits to which other ingredients, including a flavouring, are added. The flavouring consists of, inter alia, vanilla extract (which has an alcohol content of 0.6%). After the ingredients making the flavouring have been combined in their respective quantities, the flavouring has an alcohol content of 0.002%. The parties disagreed on whether the ingredients added to the wine spirits were non-alcoholic, with Diageo (the taxpayer) contending that they were and the South African Revenue Service (SARS) contending that they were not. The dispute turns on the interpretation of the aforementioned phrase in the legislation. Preceding the appeal to the SCA, the full bench of the high court, taking the relevant provision’s purpose and context into account, held that as the alcohol content contributed by the vanilla was so minute, it could be ignored by virtue of the application of the de minimis non curat lex principle. This decision was, however, overturned on appeal, with the SCA holding that the phrase’s wording is “plain and unambiguous” and that “non-alcoholic” should thus be given its ordinary, grammatical meaning of “containing no alcohol”. The SCA thus concludes that both the vanilla and the flavouring are “alcoholic”. Accordingly, it upheld SARS’s classification and as such, CVCO does not qualify for the lower excise duty rate. The SCA was unwilling to apply the de minimis principle, which we argue is wrong. Furthermore, we highlight some errors and inconsistencies in the SCA judgment and assert that the SCA did not correctly apply the prevailing approach to statutory interpretation laid out by the Constitutional Court. Finally, we offer a word of caution as to the potential broader implications of the interpretative approach as applied by the SCA in this case and appeal to the Constitutional Court to bring sobriety back to the courts’ application of the unitary approach to statutory interpretation.

item.title: [Obiter] Social Media Misconduct and Defamation Insights From Booysen v Major [2021] ZAWCHC 273
item.dc:creator: Serone Stal
item.description: This case note examines the issue of defamation in the context of social media misconduct, which can have profound legal implications for both employees and employers. Labour laws have limited explicit provisions for social media defamation but are gradually evolving to address this gap. This case note aims to assess the current state of Labour laws in context of technological advancements and explore potential legal developments to effectively manage the complexities of social media misconduct, focusing on defamation. The case note will primarily focus on the South African case of Booysen v Major and Another (5043/2021) [2021] ZAWCHC 273 ( 31 August 2021). This landmark case involving an employees defamatory social media posts had significant legal implications. The court ruling highlighted the importance of employer social media policies and the potential consequences of non-compliance, pointing towards potential legal developments in this area.

item.title: [Obiter] Dismissal for Gross Insubordination Through the Lens of Association of Mineworkers and Construction Workers Union obo Mkhonto v Commission for Conciliation, Mediation and Arbitration
item.dc:creator: Veronique Tatchell
item.description: Insubordination is widely known as one of the forms of misconduct for which an employee may be dismissed and has extensively been explored. Despite the wealth of literature on the subject, uncertainties remain regarding the precise definition of insubordination and the thresholds that warrant dismissal as a consequence. While the Labour Relations Act does not explicitly define insubordination, it does acknowledge the potential for dismissal in cases of gross insubordination. This note delves into the courts' definition of insubordination, examining the circumstances under which an employee may be dismissed for such conduct. Drawing insights from the case of Association of Mineworkers and Construction Workers Union OBO Mkhonto v Commission for Conciliation, Mediation and Arbitration ((2023) 44 ILJ 1046 (LC)) (hereafter referred to as AMCU obo Mkhonto v CCMA) this exploration aims to shed light on the uncertainties surrounding gross insubordination. Furthermore, the note addresses concerns related to overtime work that surfaced in the aforementioned case, offering insights into the legislative framework surrounding overtime, as well as dismissal. The note also considers the decisions in various cases dealing with dismissal for gross insubordination, providing recommendations for the mitigation of incorrect findings, and concludes with the way forward.

item.title: [PELJ] An Overview and Critique of the Labour Courts' Interpretation and Application of Protection Against Indirect Forms of Unfair Discrimination as Provided for in South Africa's Employment Equity Act
item.dc:creator: Elsabé Huysamen
item.description:
Unfair discrimination is deeply woven into the fabric of South African society. In the post-apartheid constitutional era, the Constitution guarantees the right to equality in the pursuit of "the full and equal enjoyment of all rights and freedoms". This reflects the adoption of substantive equality, which goes beyond mere formal equality. The constitutional right to equality is grounded in two constitutionally mandated mechanisms: affirmative action, and the prohibition of unfair discrimination. Within the broader transformative vision of the Constitution, the prohibition of unfair discrimination plays a dual role: it serves as a baseline for the defence of formal equality; and it acts as a tool of transformation, particularly through the protection against indirect unfair discrimination. Protection against indirect unfair discrimination is also provided in section 6(1) of the Employment Equity Act.

In a transformative context, protection against indirect discrimination is particularly significant because it recognises that equal treatment can sometimes perpetuate inequality. By uncovering and dismantling hidden barriers and power structures in the workplace, protection against indirect unfair discrimination plays a crucial role in fostering substantive equality and driving long-term, systemic change.

Yet, despite its transformative potential, the application of protection against indirect unfair discrimination in South African labour jurisprudence has been limited. Against the aforesaid background, the article provides an overview of the approach adopted by South African labour courts to the protection against indirect unfair discrimination under South African labour law, while ultimately critiquing it.

item.title: [Obiter] Impact of Prior Sale Agreement on Intention to Transfer Ownership of Land - Melelwe v Songca [2024] ZAGPJHC 42
item.dc:creator: Reghard Brits
item.description: The court in Melelwe v Songca ([2024] ZAGPJHC 42) set aside a contract of sale and ordered the cancellation of a deed of transfer pertaining to land under circumstances where two sale agreements had been entered into with respect to the same property. The property had been transferred to the second purchaser, but the court ordered the cancellation of the deed of transfer on the basis that a previous sale agreement had been concluded with the first purchaser, and the transferor therefore had no right to dispose of the property and could not have intended to transfer ownership to the second purchaser. After summarising the facts and findings of the court, this article sets out some background principles on the sale and transfer of land and their application to double sales. The court’s reasoning is then analysed, and the author argues that although the court explained the abstract system accurately, it misconstrued the meaning of “intention to transfer” and did not give enough weight to the core differences between a contract of sale and a transfer of ownership, particularly in the context of double sales. Since the case concerned a transfer of property from a deceased estate, some principles in this respect are also summarised.

item.title: [Obiter] The Power of Judges to Vary the Terms of a Settlement Agreement Unilaterally: The Way Forward - Mafisa v Road Accident Fund [2024] ZACC 4
item.dc:creator: Chantal Badul, Darren Subramanien
item.description:
The Constitutional Court in Mafisa v Road Accident Fund ([2024] ZACC 4) is an important judgment for legal practitioners, academics and litigants as the court addressed a significant legal issue regarding the authority of judges to amend settlement agreements unilaterally.

This case note aims to discuss the value of settlement agreements generally in litigation matters. The note also provides guidance on the role that judges play when settlement agreements are reached and proposed by litigants in light of the judgment in Mafisa v Road Accident Fund.

item.title: [Obiter] Airline Liability for Damaged Luggage and Section 65(2) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2008
item.dc:creator: AM Tait
item.description:
A public spat between an aggrieved passenger and South African airline FlySafair has raised the issue of who is liable for damage caused to the baggage of the airline’s passengers. According to the report, the passenger alleged that her brand-new, expensive suitcase was destroyed when she received it after her FlySafair flight to Cape Town International Airport. Upon approaching the airline for compensation for the damages, the passenger was advised that her claim was declined under the terms and conditions of the consumer agreement entered into between the parties.
The stance of the airline is that it is not able to accept liability for damage to luggage when such luggage, although received by the airline, must be surrendered to the system that manages luggage at the airports. Luggage is sorted, screened and transported by parties that the airline does not employ or manage – that is, the airline has no control over the parties involved in processing luggage at the airports. The terms and conditions of the airline provide that the airline will not be liable for damage to any checked luggage unless such damage is caused by their negligence while the luggage was within their control or custody.
Air travel is a much-regulated form of travel, which complicates the process of ascribing liability for damage to luggage. When it comes to determining the liability of airlines for damaged luggage in South Africa, a distinction needs to be made between international air travel to which the 1999 Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules for International Carriage by Air (Montreal Convention) applies, and domestic travel, which is carriage performed completely within South Africa, as different rules regulate each of these forms of air travel. To add to an already complicated situation, the Consumer Protection Act (68 of 2008) (CPA) contains provisions, such as section 65(2), that may play a role in assigning liability in a situation where a passenger's baggage is damaged. This provision imposes liability on suppliers in possession of a consumer’s property to compensate the consumer for any losses resulting from the supplier not acting in accordance with the prescripts of the section.
This note considers the rules regulating the liability of airlines for damaged baggage in terms of the Montreal Convention and those applicable to domestic air travel, referring to the terms and conditions of FlySafair specifically. Thereafter, section 65(2) of the CPA is considered within the context of domestic air travel to determine whether this provision applies to damaged baggage and the consequences such application may hold for both consumer and service provider, respectively. The aim is to provide a view as to whether an airline, under its duty of care provided for in section 65(2) of the CPA, is liable for damage to baggage when the airline has taken possession of a passenger’s baggage even when the baggage is handled by parties other than the airline itself before it is delivered to the passenger at the airport of destination.

item.title: [Obiter] Artificial Intelligence: Shaping the Future of the Legal Profession
item.dc:creator: Desan Iyer, Lizelle Ramaccio Calvino
item.description: The role of artificial intelligence (AI) in day-to-day work has grown exponentially in recent years, and the drastic shift from the traditional mode of carrying out tasks and functions to embedding state-of-the-art technology into everything we do has become inevitable. The COVID-19 pandemic ignited the legal profession into rethinking, revamping and redesigning a traditionally formal system into one that was more contemporary, with the focus on innovation, evolution and creativity in modern times. The trend of evolution, creativity, and digitalisation has continued post-COVID, and the emergence of artificial intelligence in most sectors worldwide has seen computers impersonate human activities and change the way the world operates. The evolution of machine learning, computing power and the Internet through artificial intelligence, which is at the core of the fourth industrial revolution, has seen the need to continue revamping and rethinking the way we do things when operating in these changing times. AI, through technology, has seen knowledge machines move beyond analytical to predictive and prescriptive applications, shaping the new economy and marketplace. There is no doubt that AI is also transforming the legal profession in ways that one can hardly imagine. This note looks at the impact of AI on legal practice, highlighting the opportunities for greater efficiency, productivity and accuracy while also looking at some of the challenges posed by AI, such as privacy issues and ethical considerations. In addition, the note looks at how AI can be incorporated into the LLB curriculum with a strong focus on deep and lifelong learning for law students. The note concludes with a recommendation for the legal sector and all parties involved in advancing the legal profession to embrace AI while mitigating its potential risks.

item.title: [Obiter] Unmarried Fathers – Do They (Still) Get a Raw Deal? The Constitutionality of the Legal Position of the Unmarried Father in South African Law
item.dc:creator: Brigitte Clark, Ruth T Nyamadzawo
item.description: With the widespread prevalence of non-marital childbearing and given the number of unmarried fathers in many South African families, the legal position of unmarried fathers in South Africa raises serious concerns about equality and the best interests of the child. Despite recent changes in legislation in South Africa, it appears that unmarried fathers’ involvement and parenting remain minimal, with South Africa having high rates of paternal absence in the lives of its children. This absence and lack of paternal involvement in children’s lives is generally not in the psychological best interest of children. Teenage pregnancy, migration, poverty, cultural and customary law and disputative relationships between parents have led to the absence of fathers in many families, resulting in no meaningful involvement from a social or economic perspective. In this article, the legal position of unmarried fathers in South Africa is examined. The current legislative position needs to give effect to the child’s international and constitutional right to parental care while balancing the interests of parents and children and acknowledging the broader trends and context of family life and caring responsibilities in these countries. It is argued that a legislative assignment of automatic responsibilities and rights will not be enough to change the current culture on the position of many unmarried fathers, but may encourage a gradual shift in the attitude of younger unmarried fathers to involvement in and responsibilities for their children’s welfare. More must be done to promote and support the concept and the implications of paternal parental responsibility in both countries. Ultimately, a sensitive and holistic approach is required – one that focuses parents and families on the significance of the child’s best interests and the importance of caring involvement from both parents.

item.title: [Obiter] Whither the Khoisan With the Khoisan Act 3 of 2019? Is the Noongar Settlement Down Under a Preferable Process?
item.dc:creator: George Barrie
item.description: Self-determination is no longer seriously challenged as a right under international law. This has been confirmed by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) and in South African case law. Since the 1960s, the international-law debate relating to self-determination has, to a large extent, been dominated by claims of indigenous peoples to self-determination. This debate culminated in the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP), which has been overwhelmingly endorsed by members of the UN General Assembly. In practice, self-determination nowadays means internal self-determination, which must be distinguished from external self-determination, such as secession, which is extremely rare. Internal self-determination comprises the right of an indigenous people living in a sovereign state to determine freely their political status and freely pursue their economic, social and cultural development. The terms “indigenous people” and “indigenous community” have become synonymous with “ethnocultural people” or “ethnocultural community”, and the distinctions between the two are no longer watertight. It is submitted that the main purpose of the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act 3 of 2019 (Khoisan Act) is aimed at the Khoisan as an ethnocultural community, although this is not evident in the Preamble of the Act. In discussing the Khoisan Act, attention is paid to its serious deficiencies. A brief reference is made to the Hungarian Roma, where an institutionalised exercise similar to that of the Khoisan Act has been embarked upon. It is a moot point whether the Khoisan Act achieves its objectives. It is proposed that the perceived objectives of the Khoisan Act can be better achieved by following the example of the Noongar Settlement in Western Australia, which has become a valuable case study on the recognition of minority rights.

item.title: [Obiter] Characterisation of Restrictive Horizontal Practices under Competition Law (Part 2)
item.dc:creator: Jan-Louis van Tonder
item.description: It is settled in South African competition law that any conduct alleged to have contravened section 4(1)(b) of the Competition Act must be properly characterised in order to ascertain whether the conduct in question falls squarely within the ambit of section 4(1)(b). In other words, it must be ascertained whether the impugned conduct, properly characterised, is the kind of conduct that is to be prohibited per se under section 4(1)(b) and that there is no scope for justification. The main aim of this series of three articles is to review characterisation under section 4(1)(b) of the Competition Act, and to assess what it involves. Part 1 critically reviews the applicable South African framework and principles relevant to characterisation as emerged in American Natural Soda Ash Corporation v Competition Commission (ANSAC) and Competition Commission v South African Breweries Ltd (SAB), and assesses the approach to whether conduct is anti-competitive by object or effect under article 101 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. Part 2 builds on Part 1 by reviewing and assessing key facets of characterisation that have further emerged from the South African case law since the ANSAC and SAB cases. Part 3 reviews and assesses the approach relevant to characterisation of restraints of trade developed in Dawn Consolidated Holdings (Pty) Ltd v Competition Commission. (Van Tonder “Characterisation of Restrictive Horizontal Practices under Competition Law (Part 1)” 2025 46(4) Obiter 872–886)
